draft.title: Naming hydrocarbons
card: An IUPAC name is built from parts. The stem shows the longest continuous carbon chain: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6).
The ending shows the bonds in the chain: -ane for only single bonds, -ene for a double bond, -yne for a triple bond.
A branch is a group attached to the main chain, named with a prefix such as methyl (one carbon) or ethyl (two carbons).
Number the chain from the end that gives the branch or bond the lowest number. That number says where it sits. In 2-methylbutane, a methyl branch is on carbon 2 of a four-carbon chain.
draft.remember: Stem for chain length, ending for bonds, numbered prefix for branches.

a.q: A hydrocarbon has an unbranched chain of five carbons with only single bonds. What is its IUPAC name?
a.why: Five carbons gives the stem pent, and only single bonds gives the ending -ane, so the name is pentane. Pentene is tempting, but -ene would mean a double bond.
a.clue: Count the carbons for the stem, then check the bonds.

b.q: A chain of four carbons has a methyl branch on carbon 2, and all bonds are single. Which name is correct?
b.why: The longest chain has four carbons (butane) and the methyl branch sits on carbon 2. 3-methylbutane is wrong because the chain is numbered from the end giving the lowest number. Butene would need a double bond.
b.clue: Number from the end that gives the branch the lower number.
